questions.question: This Virginian wrote the Declaration of Independence, doubled the nation's size with the Louisiana Purchase, and preferred to be remembered as a founder of the University of Virginia.
This president led the Union through the Civil War, issued the Emancipation Proclamation, and delivered a famously brief address at Gettysburg.
This movement's best-known bus boycott began after Rosa Parks refused to give up her seat in Montgomery, Alabama.
This 19th-century purchase from Russia added a vast northern territory that critics initially mocked as a frozen folly.
This amendment abolished slavery in the United States after the Civil War.
This Boston protest turned taxed tea into harbor water and helped push the colonies toward revolution.
This president warned against 'entangling alliances' in his Farewell Address and set the precedent of leaving office after two terms.
This president's doctrine told European powers that the Western Hemisphere was no longer open to new colonization, even though his secretary of state did much of the intellectual heavy lifting.
This muckraking novel about Chicago meatpacking helped spur federal food-safety laws, even though its author was more interested in workers than sausages.
This Supreme Court case arose from a Black man who sued for freedom after living in free territory and ended with one of the Court's most infamous rulings.
This woman escaped slavery, returned south repeatedly to guide others to freedom, and later served the Union cause during the Civil War.
This president was a former general nicknamed 'Old Hickory,' expanded presidential power, and presided over the forced removal of Native peoples from the Southeast.
This one-term president entered office with an ambitious four-part agenda, settled a northwestern boundary dispute, and left behind a war that dramatically enlarged the United States.

A young Virginia officer surrendered at Fort Necessity after an expedition into the Ohio Country helped widen a colonial dispute into the French and Indian War; decades later, his military résumé improved considerably.
This senator's name became shorthand for anti-communist accusations after televised hearings exposed just how much of his case rested on bluster.
This reformer published The North Star, escaped slavery, became a leading abolitionist speaker, and later argued forcefully for women's suffrage.
This 19th-century compromise admitted Missouri as a slave state and Maine as a free state while drawing a geographic line through the Louisiana Territory that proved anything but permanent.
This secretary of state negotiated the purchase of Alaska and survived an assassination attempt the same night Lincoln was killed.
This conqueror from Macedonia was tutored by Aristotle and built an empire stretching from Greece to India before dying in his early thirties.
This French heroine said she was guided by divine voices, helped lift the siege of Orléans, and was later burned at the stake.
This ancient Egyptian queen allied herself with both Julius Caesar and Mark Antony as Rome tightened its grip on the Mediterranean.
This empire centered on Rome once stretched from Britain to North Africa and left behind roads, aqueducts, and more political metaphors than modern republics can count.
This wall fell in 1989, becoming the most visible symbol of the collapse of communist rule in Eastern Europe.
This pandemic swept through Europe in the 14th century, killing an enormous share of the population and reshaping medieval society.
This emperor crowned himself ruler of France, reshaped European law, and met his final major defeat near a Belgian village.
This 1215 charter forced an English king to accept limits on royal authority and became a surprisingly durable symbol of the rule of law.
This Indian leader used mass civil disobedience and a famous salt march to challenge British rule without building his movement around armed revolt.
This empire's rulers called themselves Roman emperors from Constantinople long after the western empire disappeared, and endured until the city fell in 1453.
This Chinese dynasty gave its name to the country's largest ethnic group and oversaw major expansion along the Silk Road.
This North African general crossed the Alps with elephants and handed Rome one of its worst battlefield defeats at Cannae.
This Prussian statesman used wars against Denmark, Austria, and France to help unify Germany, then spent years trying to preserve the balance he had upset.
This Haitian revolutionary was born enslaved, became the dominant leader of the revolution, and died in a French prison before independence was formally declared.
This Russian ruler crushed the Streltsy, built a new capital on the Baltic, and tried to drag his country westward by force, shipbuilding, and occasionally beard taxes.
This conference of 1884–85 set rules for European claims in Africa and became shorthand for carving up a continent without much concern for the people already living there.
This Mughal emperor commissioned a white marble mausoleum for his wife, a monument whose beauty has rather outlived the imperial finances it strained.
This South American liberator helped free Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, and Bolivia, only to watch his dream of a durable continental union unravel.
This country is shaped like a boot, contains Rome and Venice, and has Sicily just off its toe.
This river runs through Egypt and helped sustain one of the world's earliest great civilizations.
This country is home to Mount Fuji, the cities of Tokyo and Kyoto, and an island chain stretching along the Pacific Ring of Fire.
This South American country contains most of the Amazon rainforest and speaks Portuguese rather than Spanish.
This European capital is famous for the Eiffel Tower, the Louvre, and a river called the Seine.
This desert covers much of northern Africa and is the largest hot desert on Earth.
This landlocked European country is known for the Alps, four national languages, and a long tradition of political neutrality.
This European capital sits on the Danube, is known for thermal baths, and has a grand neo-Gothic parliament building facing the river.
This country controls the Bosporus, spans Europe and Asia, and has Ankara rather than Istanbul as its capital.
This country contains Petra, borders Israel and Saudi Arabia, and is ruled from Amman.
This island nation lies southeast of India and was once widely known as Ceylon.
This African country is home to the Atlas Mountains, the cities of Fez and Marrakesh, and a coastline on both the Atlantic and Mediterranean.
This French Riviera city spent centuries under rulers tied to Savoy, became definitively French in the 19th century, and gives its name to a salad built around Mediterranean ingredients.
This landlocked West African country takes its modern name from a medieval empire that lay partly beyond today's borders; Bamako is its capital.
This European country has Ljubljana as its capital, a short Adriatic coastline, and a name often confused with that of a nearby nation whose capital is Bratislava.
This mountainous country in the Caucasus is home to Lake Sevan, has Yerevan as its capital, and was the first state traditionally credited with adopting Christianity as a state religion.
This capital on the Tagus became the center of a maritime empire, was devastated by a famous 18th-century earthquake, and is known for steep streets and yellow trams.

This Central Asian country has Bishkek as its capital, is dominated by the Tian Shan mountains, and shares the enormous alpine lake Issyk-Kul with no other country because the lake lies entirely within its borders.
This planet is home to Olympus Mons, has moons named Phobos and Deimos, and is famous for its rusty red appearance.
This process lets plants use sunlight to turn carbon dioxide and water into chemical energy, with oxygen as a useful byproduct for the rest of us.
This mammal is the largest animal known to have ever lived, beating even the biggest dinosaurs for sheer mass.
This organ pumps blood through the body and has four chambers in a healthy human adult.
This force keeps planets in orbit, gives objects weight, and made Newton's falling-apple story famous whether or not the apple actually hit him.
This gas makes up most of Earth's atmosphere, even though oxygen gets most of the publicity for keeping us alive.
This scientist sailed on HMS Beagle and later proposed natural selection as a mechanism for evolution.
This layer of Earth lies beneath the crust, is mostly solid rock that can flow over long timescales, and drives much of plate tectonics through convection.
This particle has no electric charge, lives in atomic nuclei, and helps explain why isotopes of the same element can have different masses.
This moon of Saturn has a thick nitrogen-rich atmosphere and lakes of liquid methane and ethane on its surface.
This molecule carries genetic instructions using four chemical bases and a double-helix structure.
This boundary around a black hole marks the point beyond which light cannot escape, giving astronomy one of its more ominous terms.
This Austrian physicist lent his name to an exclusion principle that helps explain electron structure and why ordinary matter does not collapse into itself.
This biologist's experiments with pea plants revealed patterns of inheritance decades before chromosomes gave genetics a physical mechanism.
This giant Pacific weather pattern begins with unusually warm surface water in the central and eastern tropical ocean and can disrupt rainfall around the globe.
This tiny organelle is often nicknamed the cell's 'powerhouse' because it produces much of a eukaryotic cell's ATP through respiration.

This geologist proposed that continents drift across Earth's surface after noticing how coastlines and fossil distributions seemed to fit together, decades before plate tectonics supplied the mechanism.
This African mammal is the only living member of its family, has a giraffe-like tongue, zebra-striped legs, and was unknown to Western science until the early 20th century.
This Kansas City tight end became a Super Bowl star and then an even bigger pop-culture figure through his relationship with Taylor Swift.
This NBA star spent his career with the Lakers, wore both 8 and 24, and called himself the 'Black Mamba.'
This Argentine soccer star won a long-awaited World Cup in 2022 after a career built around dazzling dribbles and a left foot that rarely seemed fair.
This quarterback won multiple Super Bowls with New England before finishing his career in Tampa Bay.
This golfer became a global superstar while still a teenager and won the Masters by a record margin in 1997.
This baseball legend broke Major League Baseball's color barrier with the Brooklyn Dodgers in 1947.
This Serbian center has collected MVP awards with Denver while cultivating a famously low-key public persona and a much-publicized love of horses.
This Buffalo quarterback starred at Wyoming, became known for a cannon arm, and has made hurdling defenders look like a reasonable career choice.
This tennis champion won 23 Grand Slam singles titles in the Open Era and built one of sports' most famous sibling rivalries with Venus.
This Formula 1 driver won seven world championships and spent his most dominant years with Mercedes.
This NHL star spent most of his career in Pittsburgh, wore 66, and returned from cancer treatment to continue one of hockey's greatest careers.
This sprinter won Olympic gold in both the 100 and 200 meters at three consecutive Games, usually with enough time to look relaxed doing it.
This shortstop was nicknamed 'The Wizard,' became synonymous with spectacular defense in St. Louis, and won his only World Series with a team built around speed and artificial turf.
This running back retired from the NFL while still near his peak, spent his entire career in Detroit, and left highlight reels full of defenders grabbing at air.
This Croatian basketball star became one of the NBA's first major European standouts, starred for the Nets, and died in a car crash at 28.
This pitcher threw a perfect game in the 1956 World Series, the only one in World Series history.
This American runner won the first Olympic marathon held in the United States, taking gold in St. Louis during one of the strangest races in Olympic history.
This boxer handed Muhammad Ali his first professional loss, later lost the 'Thrilla in Manila,' and was known for a devastating left hook.
This actor played Iron Man across the Marvel Cinematic Universe before winning an Oscar for a very different role in Oppenheimer.
This actor played a web-slinging superhero and later became engaged to his longtime co-star Zendaya.
This fantasy series follows houses Stark, Lannister, and Targaryen fighting over a very uncomfortable-looking throne.
This director made Jaws, E.T., Jurassic Park, and several Indiana Jones films, turning blockbuster filmmaking into something of a personal hobby.
This sitcom followed six friends in New York, including Ross, Rachel, Monica, Chandler, Joey, and Phoebe.
This actor became famous as Jack in Titanic and later finally won an acting Oscar for The Revenant.
This director began with low-budget crime films before making a mafia epic whose wedding, baptism, and horse-head scenes became cinematic shorthand.
This actress played Hermione Granger, later starred in Beauty and the Beast, and studied at Brown University between film projects.
This HBO series centered on a New Jersey mob boss whose therapy sessions were nearly as important as his criminal business.
This filmmaker followed Memento with Batman, dreams within dreams, interstellar travel, and a biographical epic about the atomic bomb.
This actress became a star as Rue in Euphoria after first building a younger fan base on the Disney Channel.
This 1970s film about a New York cab driver gave cinema the line 'You talkin' to me?' and one of Robert De Niro's defining performances.
This actor was working as a carpenter when he read lines during auditions for a space opera and accidentally made himself difficult to imagine replacing as its roguish smuggler.
This director moved from low-budget exploitation films to The Terminator, Aliens, Titanic, and a blue-skinned alien franchise that turned box-office records into a recurring personal challenge.
This Japanese director made Rashomon, Seven Samurai, and Ikiru, influencing generations of filmmakers from westerns to space operas.
This actor's breakout role as a boxer from Philadelphia led to a franchise, but he also created another long-running series centered on a traumatized Vietnam veteran.
This television creator co-created Twin Peaks, directed Blue Velvet and Mulholland Drive, and made surreal dread feel strangely at home in small-town America.
This actress won an Oscar for playing Queen Anne's close companion in The Favourite and later played Queen Elizabeth II on television.
This singer's Eras Tour turned a career-spanning concert into a global phenomenon and made friendship bracelets part of the dress code.
This singer built a career on hits like 'Umbrella' before expanding into fashion and beauty with Fenty.
This Liverpool band featured John, Paul, George, and Ringo and helped turn 'Beatlemania' into an actual word.
This singer was known as the 'King of Pop' and released Thriller, one of the best-selling albums ever.
This rapper's 2000s rise included The College Dropout, Late Registration, and Graduation.
This British singer turned heartbreak into massive hits including 'Someone Like You' and 'Hello.'
This band took its name from a Muddy Waters song and built its identity around the songwriting partnership of Mick Jagger and Keith Richards.
This singer went from Disney Channel fame to a blockbuster debut single about a driver's license and a breakup.
This rapper from Compton released good kid, m.A.A.d city and later became the first non-classical, non-jazz musician to win the Pulitzer Prize for Music.
This British band made an album called The Dark Side of the Moon and became famous for elaborate concept records and enormous live productions.
This singer fronted No Doubt before launching a solo career full of pop hooks, fashion, and enough spelling to make 'bananas' unforgettable.
This producer helped define the sound of the Beatles' studio years and is sometimes casually called the group's 'fifth Beatle.'
This jazz trumpeter helped shape bebop, cool jazz, and fusion across several decades, making reinvention nearly as central to his reputation as the horn itself.
This singer-songwriter wrote 'A Case of You,' painted many of her own album covers, and made the album Blue a touchstone for generations of confessional songwriting.
This producer and musician helped pioneer ambient music, worked with Roxy Music, and later became a go-to studio collaborator for artists from David Bowie to U2.
This country singer wrote 'Jolene' and 'I Will Always Love You,' then used her success to build a theme park in Tennessee.
This Nigerian musician fused jazz, funk, and West African styles into Afrobeat while using marathon performances to attack military rule and corruption.
This singer became the frontman of Queen, was born Farrokh Bulsara, and turned Live Aid into one of rock's most famous performances.
This wizard attends Hogwarts, plays Quidditch, and spends several books trying not to be killed by Lord Voldemort.
This playwright created Hamlet, Macbeth, and Romeo and Juliet while contributing an impressive number of phrases to everyday English.
This novel follows Scout Finch as her father Atticus defends a Black man accused of rape in the fictional town of Maycomb.
This dystopian novel gave us Big Brother, the Thought Police, and a year that became shorthand for surveillance and authoritarianism.
This author created Sherlock Holmes, whose deductive powers became far more famous than the medical career of the man who invented him.
This epic fantasy begins with a hobbit inheriting a dangerous ring and ends with a very long walk toward a volcano.
This wealthy mystery man throws lavish Long Island parties while remaining fixated on Daisy Buchanan and a green light across the water.
This novelist worked as an ambulance driver during World War I, lived among expatriates in Paris, and later wrote about an old Cuban fisherman.
This English novelist gave us Elizabeth Bennet, Mr. Darcy, and a remarkably durable market for awkward proposals and social misunderstandings.
This Russian novel opens with one of literature's most famous unhappy-family lines and follows a married aristocrat whose affair ends disastrously.
This American poet published only a handful of poems in her lifetime, lived much of her life in Amherst, and became famous posthumously for compact, slant-rhymed verse.
This novel's narrator Nick Carraway watches wealth, longing, and self-invention collide on Long Island during the Jazz Age.
This Argentine writer filled short stories with labyrinths, mirrors, imaginary books, and philosophical puzzles, often making a few pages feel like an entire universe.
This novelist created the fictional Yoknapatawpha County and built dense, overlapping stories around the American South in books including The Sound and the Fury.
This Irish writer's modernist novel Ulysses shadows Leopold Bloom through a single day in Dublin while turning ordinary errands into an epic-scale literary experiment.
This author imagined a totalitarian future in which citizens consume a drug called soma and are engineered into castes rather than merely watched by Big Brother.
This Japanese novelist wrote Snow Country and became the first Japanese recipient of the Nobel Prize in Literature.
This term for a word formed from initial letters includes examples like NASA and NATO, but not every abbreviation qualifies.
This Renaissance artist painted the Mona Lisa and filled notebooks with studies of anatomy, machines, and ideas centuries ahead of practical engineering.
This Dutch painter is famous for swirling night skies, sunflowers, and a career that became far more celebrated after his death.
This museum in Paris is home to the Mona Lisa and occupies a former royal palace.
This Spanish artist helped pioneer Cubism and painted Guernica in response to the bombing of a Basque town during the Spanish Civil War.
This ancient Greek architectural order is the simplest of the three classical column styles, with sturdy proportions and a plain capital.
This Mexican painter turned self-portraits, physical pain, and indigenous imagery into one of the most recognizable bodies of 20th-century art.
This French painter spent years returning to water lilies, haystacks, and changing light, helping give Impressionism both its name and its visual vocabulary.
This surrealist cultivated a theatrical mustache, painted melting clocks, and treated self-promotion as almost another artistic medium.
This Norwegian artist's best-known painting shows an anguished figure beneath a swirling sky, turning existential dread into a museum-store staple.
This architect designed Fallingwater and the Guggenheim Museum in New York while insisting that buildings should grow organically from their settings.
This Viennese painter covered portraits in gold leaf and decorative patterns, most famously in The Kiss.
This Japanese printmaker created The Great Wave off Kanagawa, one image from a series devoted to views of Mount Fuji.
This American artist turned soup cans, celebrity portraits, and repetition into a style that made commercial imagery itself the subject of fine art.
This Belgian surrealist painted men in bowler hats, impossible rooms, and a famous pipe accompanied by the warning that it was not actually a pipe.
This American sculptor became famous for mobiles, turning balance, wire, and suspended shapes into artworks that move with the air around them.
This architect's unfinished basilica in Barcelona has been under construction since the 19th century and looks as if Gothic architecture discovered coral reefs.
This photographer's black-and-white landscapes of Yosemite helped make both American wilderness and the Zone System famous.
This Japanese aesthetic values imperfection, impermanence, and weathered simplicity rather than flawless polish.
This company started as an online bookstore and later became a giant in cloud computing, streaming, and delivering almost anything to your door.
This search engine company became so dominant that its name turned into a verb for looking something up online.
This social platform began as a college network, expanded worldwide, and later became the centerpiece of a company renamed Meta.
This smartphone line debuted in 2007 and helped make touchscreens, app stores, and pocket computers feel normal almost overnight.
This video-sharing site was bought by Google in 2006 and grew into a platform for creators, music videos, tutorials, and almost every imaginable niche.
This cryptocurrency was introduced under the name Satoshi Nakamoto and uses a public blockchain rather than a central bank.
This programmer co-founded Microsoft with Paul Allen and helped turn PC software into one of the world's largest businesses.
This social platform built around short videos, algorithmic discovery, and an endless vertical feed became one of Gen Z's defining apps.
This operating system began as Linus Torvalds' personal project and now quietly powers huge numbers of servers, supercomputers, and embedded devices.
This file-sharing service popularized syncing documents across devices by storing them in the cloud, making the USB drive feel suddenly less essential.
This programming language was created at Sun Microsystems, became central to enterprise software, and built its early reputation around 'write once, run anywhere.'
This website's voting system of upvotes and downvotes organizes communities called subreddits around everything from finance to frogs.
This computer scientist helped create Unix and the C programming language, leaving fingerprints on much of modern computing without becoming a household celebrity.
This company created the graphics processors that became unexpectedly central to modern AI computing after years of being best known to PC gamers.
This protocol created by Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn underpins how data is addressed and moved across the internet.
This early web browser helped popularize the graphical internet in the 1990s before losing the browser wars to Internet Explorer.
This mathematician and computer scientist proposed a test for machine intelligence and helped crack German codes during World War II.
This open-source version-control system was created by Linus Torvalds to help manage development of the Linux kernel.
This singer turned a career-spanning stadium tour into a global event and became one half of pop culture's most scrutinized football relationship.
This Kansas City tight end became famous far beyond football after dating Taylor Swift.
This actress-singer went from Disney Channel roles to chart-topping songs about heartbreak, jealousy, and one especially famous driver's license.
This actor became the MCU's Spider-Man and later formed one of Hollywood's most recognizable young couples with Zendaya.
This singer and beauty mogul built Fenty into a major brand while keeping fans waiting a very long time for another album.
This singer first broke through with 'Ocean Eyes' and built a moody pop career alongside her producer brother Finneas.
This actor's career jumped from Disney Channel fame to Euphoria and a string of major films, while her fashion appearances became events of their own.
This musician became one of the defining stars of Puerto Rican trap and reggaeton, turning Spanish-language albums into global pop events.
This actress played Wednesday Addams for Netflix after earlier appearing in the Scream franchise, making deadpan delivery a career asset.
This singer's rise from Disney fame to hits like 'Espresso' made her one of pop's most recognizable new stars of the mid-2020s.
This actor played Elvis Presley before taking on a very different kind of role as the villainous Feyd-Rautha in Dune: Part Two.
This comedian and actor co-created and starred in Abbott Elementary, turning a Philadelphia public school into one of network television's biggest recent comedy successes.
This Irish actor moved from independent films and Normal People to major roles in Aftersun and Gladiator II, becoming a favorite of prestige-film casting directors.
This chef-turned-actor became a breakout star as Richie on The Bear after years of supporting roles in shows like Girls.
This British singer-songwriter's intimate indie-pop style helped turn albums like Punisher into critical favorites before a supergroup with Julien Baker and Lucy Dacus won a wider audience.
This actor's breakout in The Bear followed earlier comedy work in Bottoms and eventually led to an Emmy-winning run as Sydney Adamu.
This rapper from Houston built a cult following before UTOPIA became a major commercial success, with massive live shows remaining central to his brand.
This actress went from playing a troubled teen on Euphoria to leading romantic comedies and a horror franchise while becoming one of Hollywood's most visible young stars.
This rapper-singer's blend of hip-hop and pop turned songs like 'Circles' and 'Sunflower' into crossover hits, while face tattoos became part of an instantly recognizable image.
This actress broke out in Stranger Things before producing and starring in Enola Holmes, all before reaching the age when most people finish college.
